headline: NVIDIA and Eclypsium team up to fight hidden AI server hacks that survive reinstalls
summary: Eclypsium and NVIDIA are collaborating to secure AI infrastructure at the firmware and system management layers, preventing persistent attacker access that bypasses typical software reinstalls. This addresses a critical, often-overlooked security vulnerability
details: Security firm Eclypsium and NVIDIA have partnered to enhance the security of AI servers, specifically targeting low-level software. This collaboration aims to prevent hackers from maintaining hidden access even after system reinstalls and data wipes.

Their focus is on critical components like firmware, baseboard controllers, accelerators, and network interfaces. These elements can provide attackers with persistent access to machines running AI models, making them prime targets for sophisticated breaches.

The initiative seeks to mitigate risks where attackers could monitor traffic, alter workloads, or survive standard software reinstalls. By securing these foundational layers, the partnership goes beyond application-level protections such as content filters and identity checks.

This work addresses firmware and supply chain security, a layer often less frequently inspected by corporate teams compared to cloud identity or endpoint software. This oversight becomes increasingly costly as specialized and expensive GPU servers become central to AI operations.

With AI data centers consolidating compute power, each rack now holds higher-value models and data, significantly raising the stakes of a single compromised training or inference cluster. Comprehensive AI infrastructure security must cover the trusted state of chips, server boards, and firmware.

If firmware is compromised, a clean application layer can still operate on an infected machine, making detection difficult. For NVIDIA, customer trust now extends to verifiable proof that accelerators and surrounding systems can be monitored for tampering.

While the collaboration has been announced, specific product details, deployment scope, and customer timelines are yet to be disclosed. Buyers will require clarity on whether protections extend beyond GPU hosts to storage, networking, and management layers.

A key challenge is integrating these firmware-level controls without introducing prohibitive power consumption, latency, or cost penalties. Such factors are crucial for widespread adoption by cloud providers and hyperscalers.

headline: Proton goes all in on AI, tracking code generation and halting engineer hires
summary: Proton is implementing drastic measures to accelerate AI adoption, including tracking AI code generation and planning to halt traditional engineer hires after this year, focusing solely on AI builders.
details: Proton's CEO, Andy Yen, has established an email address for employees to report any obstacles to AI adoption, vowing to "ruthlessly smash everything that stands in the way of AI velocity." This initiative underscores a strong organizational push towards integrating AI at every level.

To ensure compliance and progress, Proton has installed software on employee computers to monitor the amount of AI code being generated. This tracking mechanism highlights the company's commitment to quantifiable AI development.

Proton's CEO, Andy Yen, has announced that this year will be the last for hiring traditional engineers. The company will now exclusively recruit individuals focused on building with AI, signaling a complete shift in its talent acquisition strategy.
